area: Area VII. Takeoffs, Landings, and Go-Arounds
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain and demonstrate a forward slip and a sideslip to a landing from the right seat, pick the right slip for the wind, brief the POH limits on slips, and spot and fix the slip errors learners make most.
why: A slip lets a pilot lose height without gaining speed, fix ground track in a crosswind, and reach a field in a real engine failure faster than flaps can [[24:183|AFH 9-12]] [[24:185|AFH 9-14]]. It is also the most cross-controlled thing your learners will do near the ground, the airspeed indicator may lie during it, and some airplanes limit it for fuel or flap reasons [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. You have to teach it so the learner trusts it, respects it, and knows when not to use it.

prereading.what: Intentional slips, sideslip and forward slip, the practical slip limit, exiting a slip, airspeed error, slip limitations, forward slip to a landing and its common errors.
prereading.label: AFH 9-12 to 9-15

prereading.label: AFH 9-15 to 9-19

prereading.what: The throttle as total energy control, the elevator as energy distribution control, and the energy error matrix.
prereading.label: AFH 4-4 to 4-12

prereading.what: Stabilized approach criteria and the go-around gates.
prereading.label: AFH 9-6

prereading.what: Why the horizontal tail normally pushes down (tail download from downwash). Pair it with AFH 9-2 on how flaps change downwash on the tail. The tailplane stall pages (IFH 4-15 to 4-16) are about ice on the tail.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-16

prereading.what: Instructor tells, instructor does; guarding the controls; distractions and stall/spin accidents.
prereading.label: AIH 9-7 to 9-9

prereading.what: Managing risk while teaching landings: no mechanical teaching, concise prompting on final, strong-wind skill.
prereading.label: AIH 10-9

warmup: Think first: your learner is 300 feet high on a short final with the throttle already closed and full flaps out. They push the nose over and the airspeed climbs 15 knots. What did that push actually do to the airplane's energy, and what tool would have removed height without adding speed? Now suppose the POH says to avoid slips with full flaps. What is left?

key_terms.def: Flight with the bank too steep for the rate of turn. Intentional slips lose height without adding speed or fix ground track in a crosswind [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
A slip in which the airplane keeps moving the way it was going, but its longitudinal axis is at an angle to that path [[24:379|AFH G-7]].
A slip in which the longitudinal axis stays parallel to the original path, but the horizontal part of lift moves the airplane sideways toward the low wing [[24:385|AFH G-13]].
Aileron one way and rudder the other. An intentional slip usually needs it throughout, because most airplanes tend to straighten out of a slip on their own [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].
The steepest slip possible because rudder travel runs out; more bank past it turns the airplane even with full opposite rudder [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:384|AFH G-12]].
Error in the airspeed indicator, altimeter or VSI caused by the air at the static system entrance not being still [[1:499|PHAK G-23]].
In uncoordinated flight fuel is forced to one side of a tank and can leave the pickup, starving the engine; the reason some POHs limit slips in duration or by fuel quantity [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

The slight downward force on the horizontal tail, set by its small negative angle of attack and the wing's downwash, that balances the nose-heavy airplane [[1:113|PHAK 5-16]]. Flap extension may change the downwash on the tail and alter this force [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].
A stall of the horizontal tail, which gives an uncommanded nose-down pitch. The FAA texts describe it with ice on the tail and flaps extended [[23:92|IFH 4-15]] [[23:93|IFH 4-16]].
Right total energy, wrong split: altitude and speed off in opposite directions. Fixed with the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
The sideways force on the landing gear when the airplane touches down drifting or not aligned with its path [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

chunks.title: What the slip is for, and the standard you hold

body.p: Purpose: intentional slips lose altitude without increasing airspeed, adjust ground track in a crosswind, help in forced landings and over obstacles into confined areas, and slow the airplane when flaps are inoperative or not installed [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. The AFH adds that some pilots avoid forward slips because flaps feel more familiar and the sideways push is uncomfortable, but in a real engine failure a slip starts a descent much faster than flaps, and it can be removed without penalty, while retracting flaps can cost altitude [[24:185|AFH 9-14]].

Notice the CFI Task title: “Slip to a Landing,” and K1 says forward or side slip. The private Task is “Forward Slip to a Landing” (ACS PA.IV.M). So you must be able to teach both slips and explain when each one fits.

callout.text: ACS AI.VII.M.S8: “Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift, and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway center/landing path.” Unlike the CFI normal landing (200 feet, ACS AI.VII.B.S10), this Task keeps the 400-foot window.

The Commercial ACS has no slip-to-a-landing Task of its own; forward slips appear inside its Power-Off 180° Accuracy Approach Task (CA.IV.M.R7 forward slip operations, CA.IV.M.S7 correlate crosswind with direction of forward slip). Its Appendix 1 note under the Additional Rating Task Table says evaluators must also test the private Forward Slip to a Landing Task (PA.IV.M) when the applicant does not hold an airman certificate with an airplane single-engine class rating. Ask your learners when they last flew a full slip to a landing before you assume they can.

check.q: The examiner names the touchdown point 500 feet past the threshold. What touchdown range meets your standard for this Task?
check.a: From the point to 400 feet beyond it, about 500 to 900 feet past the threshold, with no drift and the axis on the centerline (ACS AI.VII.M.S8).

chunks.title: Forward slip or sideslip: same controls, different jobs

body.p: Both slips are a lowered wing with opposite rudder. A slip moves the airplane forward and sideways toward the low wing, so it flies sideways through the air, the relative wind strikes it at an angle, drag rises sharply, and the reduced vertical lift lets it descend quickly without gaining speed [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Most airplanes have positive directional stability and try to straighten out, so the cross-control is held the whole time [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

head: Forward slip
Sideslip (wing-low)
rows: Job
Lose altitude and increase descent rate without increasing airspeed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Keep the airplane aligned with the centerline in a crosswind [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Nose
No longer points along the flightpath; yawed away from it [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Stays parallel to the original flightpath [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Rudder
Enough opposite rudder to yaw the nose the other way while staying on the original path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Just enough opposite rudder to prevent a turn [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Bank sets
The amount of slip and the sink rate: steeper bank, steeper descent [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
The rate of sideways movement: steeper bank, more slip [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]
Power
Normally idle [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
As needed for a normal approach (application)
Airspeed
Controlled with the elevator [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Normal approach speed, as in AI.VII.B

body.p: Practical slip limit: in most light airplanes rudder travel limits the slip. Once full rudder is needed to hold the heading, more bank only makes the airplane turn [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Lowering the nose past that point adds sink rate and airspeed, and the extra speed makes the rudder stronger so a steeper slip is possible. Raising the nose does the opposite, so reduce bank as you slow [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

Steering in a slip: even at full rudder, more or less aileron moves the airplane left or right of the intended track [[24:185|AFH 9-14]]. Exit: level the wings and release rudder together while setting the normal glide attitude. Releasing the rudder abruptly snaps the nose into line and the airplane picks up excess speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

callout.text: Forward slip: nose off the runway, losing height. Sideslip: nose on the runway, beating drift. Same stick and rudder directions; the amount of rudder makes the difference.

check.q: Your learner holds a forward slip at full rudder and still needs to come down faster. What can they do, and what does it cost?
check.a: Lower the nose. It adds sink rate and airspeed, and the extra speed makes the rudder stronger for a steeper slip, but the approach is now faster [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

body.p: The AFH treats the throttle as the total energy control and the elevator as the control that splits energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. Drag changes total energy too, but drag devices can only add drag, so normally thrust is the energy lever [[24:90|AFH 4-4]]. On final the AFH lists the pilot's tools for the descent angle as airspeed, attitude, power and drag, naming flaps or a forward slip as the drag [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

head: Approach picture
Energy error
Where the slip fits
rows: High, on speed, power at idle
Too much total energy [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]; at idle the throttle has nothing left to take away (application)
Add drag: flaps or a forward slip. The slip takes energy out without the pitch-down that turns height into speed (application)
High and fast
Too much total energy [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]
Power to idle first; then the slip adds drag while the elevator holds approach speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
High and slow
Distribution error [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]
Lower the nose to trade height for speed first; a slip at low speed has weaker rudder and less margin [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Low (any speed)
Too little energy or wrong split [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]
Never slip. Remove any slip at once; it only adds sink (application)

body.p: Why not just dive? Pushing toward the aiming point builds a sink rate that is hard to stop near the ground; 800 to 1,000 fpm is considered excessive. A forward slip steepens the path and raises the descent rate while holding approach speed [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. Holding that speed is the learner's job with the elevator, not the throttle [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

Sideslip energy: a sideslip adds drag and reduces vertical lift too. The AFH lists 'excessive sink rate or too low an airspeed from increased drag and reduced vertical lift during sideslip' as a crosswind landing error [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. On a long wing-low final, watch the aiming point and the speed, not a memorized power setting [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

callout.text: Removing the slip is an energy event. Drag drops at once and the airplane wants to float and accelerate, more so if the rudder is released abruptly [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Plan to be out of the slip and on speed before the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

check.q: Throttle closed, on speed, 200 feet high on a half-mile final, flaps up. What kind of energy error is it, and why is the slip a good tool here?
check.a: Too much total energy with no throttle left to reduce [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. A slip adds drag and steepens the descent while the elevator holds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

chunks.title: Wind, air and runway: R2 effects on a slip approach

body.p: Atmospheric conditions change the landing even when the indicated speed is right. At a high field the airplane lands at the same indicated airspeed but a higher true airspeed, so the landing distance grows, about 16 percent at 5,000 feet compared with sea level, roughly 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Because the airplane lands at an airspeed independent of the wind, wind mainly changes the groundspeed at touchdown [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]], and it changes the gliding distance over the ground [[24:174|AFH 9-3]].

head: Effect of
What it does to a slip approach
What to teach
rows: Crosswind

Sets which wing goes down. Slip into the wind: lower the upwind wing, because that makes it easier to stay on the original path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Too much crosswind for full rudder means the runway is wrong [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].
Correlate the slip with the wind on every approach (ACS AI.VII.M.S7).
Windshear

A sudden, drastic change in wind speed or direction over a small area; a headwind turning to tailwind cuts airspeed, and a microburst can push the airplane down short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
A slip at idle has no power in hand. If the airspeed or sink rate jumps, add full power, take out the slip with it and go around (application of [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] and [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]).
Tailwind

About 21 percent more landing distance for a 10-knot tailwind [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. With a tailwind the airplane glides farther because of the higher groundspeed [[24:84|AFH 3-23]], so expect to overshoot the point.
A tailwind makes learners high; brief the slip as the fix and the runway length as the limit.
Wake turbulence
Vortices sink behind the generating aircraft and near the ground drift sideways; a light quartering tailwind can move them into the touchdown zone [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]] [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

Behind a larger aircraft landing on the same runway, stay at or above its path and land beyond its touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]. Application: a steep slip from above can drop you into its path.
Landing surface/condition

Snow, ice or soft ground significantly change landing distance [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]. Water cuts braking, and landing fast raises the hydroplaning risk [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. A downslope lengthens the roll [[1:269|PHAK 11-13]].
A slip that ends fast, with a long float, eats runway you may not have on a wet or short strip.

body.p: Gusty air: a power-on approach a little above normal speed gives more positive control in turbulence [[24:191|AFH 9-20]]. That fits a sideslip to the touchdown. A forward slip at idle in strong gusts leaves less margin, so many instructors save the full idle forward slip for smoother days (application).

callout.text: Teach the learner to find the wind before the slip: the windsock, the ATIS or AWOS, and the drift on base. The question 'Which wing goes down?' should be answered before turning final.

check.q: Why does a light quartering tailwind matter more than a direct crosswind when a jet has just landed ahead of you?
check.a: A light quartering tailwind can push the jet's vortices forward into the touchdown zone; the AIM says it needs maximum caution [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]]. Land beyond the jet's touchdown point [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]].

chunks.title: Planning the pattern: runway, path, point, checklist and calls

body.p: The AFH demonstration pattern: plan the descent so a forward slip can be used on final. Flaps usually stay retracted, and a slip on downwind or base may be part of it. Abeam the landing point on downwind, reduce power to idle; if the descent is not enough on downwind, slip. Make a coordinated turn to base, keep judging height, and if high, keep slipping. Make a coordinated turn to final, then use the slip to set a suitable path to the aiming point. When the round out begins, remove the slip and make a normal landing [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

bullets: Checklists (S1): finish the before-landing checks on downwind [[24:167|AFH 8-3]]. Briefings and checklists, except the landing checklist, belong before the approach [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

Radio calls (S2): at a nontowered field, report entering downwind, downwind to base and base to final [[24:170|AFH 8-6]]; say the airport name at the start and end and the runway number, never 'active runway' [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].
Flightpath (S3): plan the path considering altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions (ACS AI.VII.M.S3). Do not descend too much on a downwind with a tailwind [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].
Touchdown point (S4): pick it from wind, surface, obstructions and the airplane, not mechanically [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

Downwind (S5): parallel to the runway, about 1/2 to 1 mile out, at pattern altitude; power comes back abeam the approach end, or abeam the landing point for this maneuver [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

Configure (S6): flaps usually retracted for the demonstration [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]; power idle for the forward slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; any POH limit on slips with flaps or on slip duration comes first [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

body.p: Selection of runway/landing surface, approach path and touchdown area (R1). Pilot capability: the RMH sample personal minimums for a single-engine pilot include a 7-knot crosswind component and a 2,500-foot shortest runway [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]. Aircraft performance and limitations: know the demonstrated crosswind, shown in certification up to 0.2 VSO [[24:190|AFH 9-19]], and the POH slip limits. Available distance: the PIC must know runway lengths and the airplane's landing distance data [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]]. Wind: if full opposite rudder cannot hold the needed bank, land on a better runway or at another airport [[24:188|AFH 9-17]].

callout.text: Over an obstacle into a short field, a slip ending late leaves the airplane fast and floating with little runway. For a real short-field arrival, the short-field Task's stabilized path is usually the better tool; save the slip for a correction (application).

check.q: Where does the AFH put the power reduction in its forward slip to a landing, and what does the pilot do if the descent on downwind is not enough?
check.a: Abeam the landing point on downwind, power to idle; if the rate of descent is insufficient, use a forward slip there [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

chunks.title: Crosswind: slip into the wind, then sideslip to touchdown

body.p: Wind correction in a forward slip: with a crosswind, lower the upwind wing so the airplane is banked into the wind; slipping into the wind makes it easier to hold the original path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Wind correction in a sideslip: rudder holds the nose on the runway direction, the airplane begins to drift, and aileron gives just enough bank to cancel the drift; vary bank to move left or right of centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

callout.text: ACS AI.VII.M.S7: “As necessary, correlate crosswind with direction of slip and transition to sideslip as appropriate before touchdown.” ACS AI.VII.M.S9: “Maintain a ground track aligned with the runway center/landing path.”

body.p: The transition. Because both slips use the same aileron and rudder directions when the forward slip is into the wind, going from forward slip to sideslip is a matter of easing rudder until the nose lines up with the runway, and setting the bank that just stops the drift (application of [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] and [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]). If the learner slipped with the downwind wing low, the controls must fully reverse at the worst moment, which is why the AFH lists 'a slip in the same direction as any crosswind' and 'late transition to a sideslip' as errors [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

head: Moment
Controls
Patter
rows: Final, high
Upwind wing down, lots of opposite rudder, nose off to the downwind side, elevator holds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
'Wind from the right, right wing down, left rudder.'
Path made
Sideslip: rudder holds the nose on the runway direction, bank just stops the drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. Easing rudder from the forward slip gets there (application)
'Nose to the runway, keep the wing down.'
Round out
Controls weaken; increase aileron and rudder gradually and keep the upwind wing down [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]
'More wing, more rudder as we slow.'
Touchdown
Upwind main first, then the downwind main [[24:188|AFH 9-17]]
'Upwind wheel, then the other.'
Rollout
More and more aileron into the wind as speed drops [[24:189|AFH 9-18]]
'Keep flying it to a stop.'

callout.text: In calm wind there is no sideslip to transition to: remove the forward slip at the round out and land normally [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. The 'as appropriate' in S7 means you must tell the examiner which case you are in.

check.q: Wind from the left. Your learner is in a forward slip on final with the right wing low. What is wrong, and what will happen at the round out?
check.a: The slip is in the same direction as the crosswind, an AFH common error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. To transition to a sideslip they must reverse both controls near the ground, so the transition is likely to be late and the touchdown drifting.

chunks.title: Forward slip operations: fuel flowage, tail stalls with flaps, airspeed control

body.p: Forward slip operations carry three risks named in R7. Two of them, fuel flowage and flaps, are airplane-specific, so the habit is the same: read the POH limitations before you teach slips in that airplane [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

head: Risk
What the sources say
What you teach
rows: Fuel flowage

Some airplanes limit slips in duration or by fuel quantity, to prevent fuel starvation when fuel is forced to one side of a tank in uncoordinated flight [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. The AFH's multiengine chapter adds that some single-engine airplanes, like some twins, have POH limits on slips beyond a set time (30 seconds is its example only), because fuel in the lowered wing's tank flows toward the tip, away from the pickup [[24:271|AFH 13-22]].

Brief the number in your POH; 30 seconds is an example, not a rule. A long wing-low final is a slip too, so the same limit counts there (the AFH says so for the wing-low method in its multiengine chapter [[24:271|AFH 13-22]]). In a real engine-out slip to a field, the AFH says a time or fuel limit is irrelevant unless a prolonged slip caused the problem [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Tail stalls with flaps

The AFH slip section says only that, for aerodynamic reasons, there may be recommendations or limitations on slips with flaps extended, and to consult the AFM/POH [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Flap deployment may change the wing's downwash on the horizontal tail and alter the tail-down force, so pitch behavior with flaps depends on the design; beyond 15° some high-wing airplanes get a significant nose-up pitching moment [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The tail normally pushes down [[1:113|PHAK 5-16]]. No AFH or PHAK page describes a tail stall in a clean (ice-free) airplane slipping with flaps.

Follow the POH note on slips with flaps; if it limits them, practice at the flap settings it allows or flaps up, as in the AFH demonstration [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. If the POH is silent, say so to the examiner and don't invent a rule. The IFH tailplane stall symptoms and recovery are for ice on the tail [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]; don't teach them as the clean-airplane slip risk.
Airspeed control

Because of where the pitot tube and static vents are, some airspeed indicators have considerable error in a slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Installation and instrument errors can total several knots and are greatest at low airspeeds [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].
Recognize a good slip by attitude, the sound of the airflow and the feel of the controls [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Hold the pitch attitude you know; don't chase the needle.

body.p: Why the airspeed lies: position error is the error caused by air at the static system entrance not being still [[1:499|PHAK G-23]]. In a slip the airplane flies sideways through the air [[24:183|AFH 9-12]], so the static port on one side meets moving air. The size and direction of the error depend on the airplane; the sources do not give numbers. Reacting to erroneous airspeed indications is on the AFH error list [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

The ball is a recognition aid, not a target here. In a slip the ball is off to the low side and the pilot feels pushed that way [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Show the learner the displaced ball once, so they know the slip is real, then get their eyes back outside.

callout.text: Icing only: the icing AC warns pilots to be alert to tailplane stall particularly after full flap deflection, on airplanes not evaluated for susceptibility, and to consider a no-flap landing consistent with the AFM [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]]. With ice on the tail, the IFH recovery is to retract the flaps to the previous setting with nose-up elevator [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]. This guidance is about ice-contaminated tails, not a clean airplane; but an iced airplane is no place for a flaps-down slip demonstration.

check.q: Halfway down final in a slip, the airspeed suddenly reads 12 knots lower, but the pitch attitude, wind noise and control feel are unchanged. What do you coach?
check.a: Likely slip-induced airspeed error from pitot and static location [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Hold the known attitude and judge by sound and feel; reacting to it is a listed error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

chunks.title: Touchdown: axis aligned, no drift, on the point

body.p: Surface contact with the airplane's longitudinal axis misaligned is the R8 risk this Task creates. A forward slip deliberately points the nose off the path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], so a slip held into the round out lands crooked. The touchdown should be made with the axis exactly parallel to the direction of motion; touching down turned or drifting puts severe side loads on the gear [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

When the airplane touches down drifting or crabbed, the tire tread stops the sideways motion suddenly. The resulting moment tends to tip the airplane and load one main wheel, and the wind weathervanes it toward a ground loop [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. The sideslip prevents this by keeping the track and axis on the centerline through the touchdown and rollout [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

bullets: Proper pitch attitude (S8): once the slip is removed, the round out and touchdown are the normal landing; teach and grade them as in AI.VII.B [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
On the point: a slip removed late or abruptly leaves the airplane fast and floating [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. If it will not be down in the first third or it drifts, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].
Ground track (S9): the centerline is held from final through the rollout, with aileron increasing into the wind as speed drops [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

callout.text: ACS AI.VII.M.S8 asks for no side drift and the longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway center/landing path. A forward slip still in at touchdown fails both halves of that sentence.

check.q: Your learner touches down with the nose 10 degrees right of the runway after holding the slip too long. Why does the AFH care?
check.a: Touching down turned to the path puts severe side loads on the gear [[24:180|AFH 9-9]], and the sudden stop of sideways motion tends to tip the airplane and start a ground loop [[24:206|AFH 9-35]].

body.p: Unstable approach: the AFH gates say go around if not stabilized by 500 feet above airport elevation in VMC, and in a typical light piston pattern go around at once if the approach becomes unstabilized below 300 feet AGL. Its criteria include a descent rate generally 500 to 1,000 fpm, and a pilot using more than 500 fpm should reduce it before 300 feet AGL [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]. A forward slip on short final is a correction, and the AFH text supports using it to rejoin the path from above without diving [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]; a slip that is still needed below the gate means the plan failed.

callout.text: The AFH says a go-around should be started if the sink rate becomes excessive while correcting a high final [[24:201|AFH 9-30]]. Do not let a slip become a license to continue an approach that was never going to work.

body.p: Rejected landing and go-around from a slip: power is still the first concern: the instant the decision is made, full or maximum allowable power goes in smoothly and without hesitation [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. At the same time take the slip out, leveling the wings and releasing the rudder smoothly (not abruptly) while setting the pitch attitude [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], because a slip adds a lot of drag and cuts climb performance [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Then hold the nose with forward pressure and right rudder, and retract flaps in small steps after the descent stops [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Ground effect can make a very low go-around feel better than it is [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Stress that any approach may end in a go-around and that delay comes from landing expectancy and pride [[24:182|AFH 9-11]].

Land and hold short operations (LAHSO): accept only if sure the airplane can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance; student pilots and pilots not familiar with LAHSO should not take part [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]. A LAHSO clearance does not stop you from going around [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]. Application: a slip approach that may float past the point is a poor match for a hold-short limit, so decline LAHSO for slip practice.

head: Approach state
Call
rows: High at 500 feet, slip fixes it, on speed and stable by 300 feet
Continue; remove the slip before the round out [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]
Still slipping hard at 200 feet, sink over 1,000 fpm
Airspeed rising in the slip and float expected past the first third
Go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]]
LAHSO offered during slip practice
Decline promptly [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]]

check.q: In a go-around from a forward slip, where do power and taking the slip out fit, and why?
check.a: Full power smoothly the instant you decide, because power is the first concern [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; with it, wings level and rudder released smoothly with the pitch set [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], since a slip adds a lot of drag and cuts climb performance [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. The airplane is not climbed while still cross-controlled.

chunks.title: Low and cross-controlled: stall, spin, CFIT, traffic and distraction

body.p: Low altitude maneuvering, stall and spin: the AFH says that unlike a skid, a slip that stalls shows very little of the yawing tendency that turns a skidding stall into a spin; it may do little more than roll toward wings level [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. But the AFH also warns that in a slipping turn stall the outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Teach that the slip is the better cross-control, not a safe one, and that the real killer is the skidding base-to-final turn: inside rudder, steeper bank and back pressure can roll toward inverted and spin; the fix for an overshoot is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

CFIT: causes include night, low ceilings or visibility, high density altitude and intentionally flying too low [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. A slip makes height go away fast; over unfamiliar or rising terrain, or at night, the learner can arrive low before the brain catches up (application).

Collision hazards: most reported midair collisions happen on final or short final [[24:171|AFH 8-7]]. A forward slip yaws the nose away from the runway, so the learner's view changes; brief where to look before the slip. Aircraft on final have the right-of-way, but the lower aircraft may not cut in front of one on final [[60:448|14 CFR 91.113(g)]]. A flight instructor was on board in 37 percent of the midair collisions in the AIH study [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Distractions, task prioritization, loss of situational awareness: overload shows first as working harder but getting less done, then fixating on one item [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Most stall/spin accidents happened when attention was diverted from flying, and 60 percent occurred during takeoff and landing [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. In a slip the learner is juggling aileron, rudder, pitch and a hidden airspeed indicator; your talking is one more load, so prompt briefly on final [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

Disorientation: skid, slip and uncoordinated turns feel alike, and the pilot feels pushed sideways in the seat [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. The body's sense of 'level' is unreliable in a slip. Teach eyes outside on the runway and the horizon, and a check of the attitude before releasing the slip.

callout.text: Never let a learner turn a slip into a skid in the turn to final to 'tighten it up.' Bottom rudder with bank in the turn direction is the skidding cross-control setup, not a slip [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

check.q: Your learner says, 'Slips are safe, they can't spin.' What is your more complete answer?
check.a: A stalled slip shows little of the yaw that makes a skid spin [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], but in a slipping turn the outer wing may stall first and drop [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Stay on speed, and never skid to final [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: Ground brief: draw both slips from above (the two figures earlier), name the job of each, and agree on the words you will use in the air. Brief the POH slip and flap limits for the airplane, the go-around triggers, and who has the controls. Explain the sideways push before the flight: the AIH says unfamiliar sensations are usually overcome by understanding their cause, and instructors should never ridicule a learner bothered by them [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

bullets: Build from known to unknown. The sideslip uses the same inputs as the wing-low crosswind landing; when a skill relates to one already learned, the known-to-unknown strategy works [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Many learners meet the sideslip first in crosswind work; start the forward slip from that.
Demonstrate exactly the way you want it practiced, in the same order you explained it, including the safety steps [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. If your demo needs a bigger slip than planned, say so out loud.

Patter for the demo: 'Power idle. Right wing down, left rudder, nose off to the left. Pitch holds 65 knots; I'm not watching the airspeed because it may lie in a slip. Steepen the bank, more descent. Path made: wings level, rudder out smoothly, normal glide attitude.' Adjust the numbers to the POH.
Practice up high first: slips can be entered, steepened and exited with no runway pressure. Then bring them to the pattern.
In the pattern, teach the slip as a correction, not a script. The AIH warns that teaching landings mechanically leaves learners unable to manage changing conditions [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
Vary it: put the learner high on purpose, with different winds and sides, so the decision 'which wing, how much, when out' is practiced, not just the motion [[25:78|AIH 3-27]].

head: Moment
Let them work it
Take it, or call the go-around
rows: Slip entry
A shallow slip or slow rudder, on speed
Nose pitching down with speed building fast, or a turn developing toward a skid [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Short final
A little late on the exit with time to recover
Still slipping and sinking hard below the gate [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]
Round out
A small crab or drift being corrected
Landing with the axis well off the runway or drifting [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]

body.p: Guard the controls throughout, take them calmly with 'I have the flight controls,' and never let a learner go past your own ability to perceive, decide and react [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]. In strong winds you need the skill for those winds yourself [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

check.q: Your learner is uneasy every time you slip and keeps leveling the wings early. What does the AIH suggest you do?
check.a: Don't ignore or ridicule it; explain the cause of the sensation, since such sensations are usually overcome by understanding them [[25:163|AIH 8-5]], then build from the familiar wing-low crosswind inputs [[25:177|AIH 9-7]].

body.p: The AFH lists eight common errors for forward slips to a landing [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. On the checkride the examiner may fly one as your learner. Name it, say what caused it, and reteach it (ACS AI.VII.M.S10).

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Incorrect pitch adjustments that result in poor airspeed control
Nose bobbing in the slip, speed creeping up as bank increases
Hold a fixed pitch attitude with the elevator; speed is controlled with elevator in a forward slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Reacting to erroneous airspeed indications
Learner pulls up or pushes over when the needle jumps on slip entry
Teach attitude, sound and control feel as the cues [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Using excess power while trying to lose altitude
Throttle cracked open in a forward slip; path stays flat
Power to idle for the forward slip [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
A slip in the same direction as any crosswind
Downwind wing low, drift building, big heading changes to stay on centerline
Lower the upwind wing; slipping into the wind holds the path [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]
Poor glidepath control
Slip in, slip out, path above then below the aiming point
Vary bank to set the descent; steeper bank, steeper descent [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; watch the aiming point [[24:176|AFH 9-5]]
Late transition to a sideslip during landing with crosswinds
Nose still yawed off at the round out, drift at touchdown
Ease rudder to line up and set bank for drift before the round out [[24:187|AFH 9-16]] [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]
Landing without the longitudinal axis parallel to runway
Tires chirp sideways, airplane jerks or swerves at contact
Axis parallel to the motion at touchdown [[24:180|AFH 9-9]]; go around if you cannot get there
Landing off the centerline
Touchdown on one side; learner fixed the slip but not the track
Vary bank in the sideslip to move to the centerline [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]

body.p: Two errors the AFH names outside that list belong in your watch list too. Abrupt rudder release on exit swings the nose into line and adds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. And sinking 800 to 1,000 fpm or more while correcting from high is excessive and calls for a go-around [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

callout.text: Ask before you tell. 'Which wing did you lower, and where was the wind?' finds the crosswind error faster than your explanation. A learner who can describe the slip but still needs your help to fly it is at the AIH 'describe' or 'explain' level, not 'perform' [[25:137|AIH 6-6]].

check.q: Your learner's slips always end with the airplane floating far past the point. Which two causes do you look for first?
check.a: Abrupt rudder release, which swings the nose and adds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], and incorrect pitch that let the speed build during the slip [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

f1.caption: Figure 9-14. Forward slip. (AFH 9-14)
f1.alt: Top view of a high-wing airplane over a runway. The black arrow for the direction of movement points straight up the runway, and the relative wind arrow points straight down it, but the airplane's nose is yawed well to the right of that path, so the fuselage sits at a large angle to the runway.

f2.caption: Figure 9-13. Sideslip. (AFH 9-13)
f2.alt: Top view of the same airplane over a runway with its nose and fuselage pointed straight along the runway centerline and the direction of movement arrow straight ahead, while the relative wind arrow comes in at an angle from the upper left.

f3.caption: Figure 9-16. Sideslip approach. (AFH 9-16)
f3.alt: View from behind a high-wing trainer on short final to runway 08 in a crosswind from the right. The airplane is banked with the right wing low toward the wind streamer, the nose lines up with the runway centerline, and the right main wheel hangs lower than the left.

f4.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid. (AFH 3-13)
f4.alt: Three panels: skid, coordinated turn and slip. Each shows an attitude indicator in a right bank, a turn coordinator, and a seat with a red arrow. In the skid the ball is to the outside of the turn and the pilot feels pushed outward; coordinated, the ball is centered and the force is straight down into the seat; in the slip the ball is to the inside of the turn and the pilot feels pushed toward the inside.

f5.caption: Figure 4-22. Downward force on the tailplane. (IFH 4-15)
f5.alt: Side view of a light airplane with arrows: center of lift pointing up near the wing, weight pointing down at the center of gravity just ahead of it, and a tail download arrow pointing down at the horizontal tail.

f6.caption: Figure 17-6. Sensations from centrifugal force. (PHAK 17-8)
f6.alt: Six front views of a pilot silhouette in an airplane with a red arrow showing the felt force: level, coordinated turn and pull out all press straight into the seat; level skid, forward slip and uncoordinated turn press the pilot sideways. The caption says skid, slip and uncoordinated turns feel similar.

f7.caption: Figure 9-37. Drifting during touchdown. (AFH 9-35)
f7.alt: Front view of a high-wing airplane touching down while drifting, with wind from the right. Arrows show wind force on the side, inertia force at the center of gravity, weight, and the tire's force resisting side motion, which together tend to tip the airplane and raise the upwind wing.

scenario.title: Slip lesson at a short, wet field with a crosswind
scenario.setup: You are teaching a private learner forward slips at a nontowered field, runway 27, 2,600 feet, wet after a shower. Wind 230 at 10. The trainer's POH has a note limiting slips with flaps extended. A twin just landed and is clearing the runway. Showers are building 15 miles to the west. Your learner wants to do the slips with full flaps 'to make it more realistic.'

questions.q: Which wing goes down in the forward slip, and what will the learner need to do before the round out?
questions.a: Wind from 230 on runway 27 is a left crosswind, so the left wing goes down: slipping into the wind makes the path easier to hold [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Before touchdown, ease the rudder into a sideslip with the left wing still low (ACS AI.VII.M.S7) [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

questions.q: What do you say about full flaps?
questions.a: No. Follow the POH note; the AFH says there may be limitations on slips with flaps for aerodynamic reasons [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], and flaps can change downwash and tail-down force [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. The AFH demonstration keeps flaps usually retracted [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

questions.q: Is a wet, 2,600-foot runway a concern for slip practice?
questions.a: Yes. A slip that ends fast floats, wet runways cut braking and fast landings raise hydroplaning risk [[1:270|PHAK 11-14]]. Check POH distance against the runway [[60:440|14 CFR 91.103(b)]] and go around if not down in the first third [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

questions.q: The twin landed on your runway. What changes in your plan?
questions.a: Land beyond its touchdown point and stay at or above its path [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]; the vortices sink and drift near the ground [[34:148|AIM 7-4-4]]. Do not slip steeply below its path from above.

questions.q: On the third approach the airspeed jumps 10 knots and the airplane balloons, then sinks hard. What now?
questions.a: Possible windshear from the building showers [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. Full power at once and go around [[24:182|AFH 9-11]], taking the slip out as the power comes in [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. An unstable approach below 300 feet is a go-around in any case [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].

questions.q: Your learner holds the slip to 10 feet and touches down crabbed. What do you debrief?
questions.a: Late transition and landing without the axis parallel are both AFH errors [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]; the side load can tip the airplane and start a ground loop [[24:206|AFH 9-35]]. Ask them to describe where the nose was first, then fix the exit point.

skills.do: Complete the before-landing checklist on downwind and the landing checklist, and explain where slip and flap limits from the POH fit in the brief.
skills.practice: Read the POH limitations section aloud before each slip lesson; do the downwind flow and say why [[24:167|AFH 8-3]] [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

skills.do: Make the pattern calls for the slip approach and explain the phraseology.
skills.practice: Script downwind, base and final calls with the airport name at both ends [[24:170|AFH 8-6]] [[33:209|AIM 4-1-9]].

skills.do: Plan and fly a path that needs a slip, considering altitude, wind, terrain and obstructions, and explain the plan.
skills.practice: Fly the AFH plan: idle abeam the point, slip as needed on downwind, base and final, out at the round out [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

skills.do: Choose a touchdown point that suits the wind, surface, obstructions and airplane, and say why.
skills.practice: Pick a new point each circuit and explain it, never by rote [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

skills.do: Fly downwind parallel to the runway at pattern altitude and spacing, and explain how the slip plan starts there.
skills.practice: Hold 1/2 to 1 mile and pattern altitude until abeam the point [[24:167|AFH 8-3]].

skills.do: Configure the airplane correctly: power idle for the forward slip, flaps as the POH allows, and explain the reasons.
skills.practice: Practice slips flaps up first, then only in flap settings the POH permits [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

skills.do: As necessary, correlate crosswind with direction of slip and transition to sideslip as appropriate before touchdown (ACS AI.VII.M.S7), while explaining which wing goes down and why.
skills.practice: On every approach, call the wind side and the low wing before turning final; time the rudder release to finish before the round out [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

skills.do: Touch down at a proper pitch attitude, within 400 feet beyond or on the specified point, with no side drift, and with the airplane’s longitudinal axis aligned with and over the runway center/landing path (ACS AI.VII.M.S8), while talking.
skills.practice: Have someone name a point; land within 400 feet past it with the slip out and the axis straight [[24:180|AFH 9-9]].

skills.do: Maintain a ground track aligned with the runway center/landing path (ACS AI.VII.M.S9) through the slip, the touchdown and the rollout.
skills.practice: Use aileron in the slip to stay on the track even at full rudder, and aileron into the wind on the rollout [[24:185|AFH 9-14]] [[24:189|AFH 9-18]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors related to this Task when the examiner flies as your learner: name the error, its cause and the fix.
skills.practice: Drill the eight AFH errors with a friend in the right seat until you can name each from what you see [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

quiz.q: Which statement about a forward slip matches the AFH?
options: The nose stays aligned with the path, and bank sets the sideways drift rate
The direction of motion stays the same, and the nose points off the path
The nose and the path both swing toward the lowered wing at a steady rate
The airplane turns toward the raised wing while descending at a constant rate
quiz.why: In a forward slip the direction of motion continues as before, but the nose no longer points along the flightpath [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: In most light airplanes, what limits how steep a slip can be?
options: Aileron travel, because the ailerons run out of deflection well before the rudder does
Elevator authority, because the nose cannot be held up once the bank passes 30 degrees
Flap setting, because the POH forbids any bank beyond 15 degrees with flaps extended
Rudder travel, because past full rudder any added bank makes the airplane turn
quiz.why: Rudder travel sets the practical slip limit; past it, more bank causes a turn [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: Exiting a forward slip, your learner snaps the rudder to neutral. What does the AFH say happens?
options: The nose swings into line too quickly and the airplane tends to gain excess speed
The upwind wing drops sharply and the airplane rolls back into a steeper slip
The stall warning sounds because angle of attack jumps when the rudder returns
Nothing harmful, since the airplane's directional stability straightens it out smoothly
quiz.why: Abrupt rudder release swings the nose too quickly into line and the airplane tends to acquire excess speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: Why do some POHs limit slip duration or fuel quantity during slips?
options: Slipping overheats the cylinders on one side because cooling air is blocked
Fuel can be forced to one side of a tank and leave the pickup, starving the engine
The fuel vents face backward in a slip and the tanks can collapse from low pressure
Long slips overload the wing root fittings once the fuel tanks are more than half full
quiz.why: The limits prevent fuel starvation from fuel forced to one side of a tank in uncoordinated flight [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

quiz.q: What role does the throttle play in the AFH energy model?
options: It controls the airplane's total energy by setting thrust against drag
It divides energy between altitude and airspeed by changing the pitch attitude
It controls only airspeed, while the elevator controls only the altitude
It controls only altitude, while the drag devices control the airspeed
quiz.why: The throttle is the total energy controller; the elevator distributes energy [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

quiz.q: Per the AFH, what else can flap extension do to pitch besides the nose-down moment from added camber?
options: Change the wing's downwash on the horizontal tail and alter the tail-down force
Move the center of gravity aft, so the tail must lift upward instead of push down
Remove all downwash from the tail, so the elevator works only in the slipstream
Set the tail's angle of attack to zero, so the tail can no longer stall at any speed
quiz.why: Flap deployment may affect wing downwash on the horizontal tail and alter the tail-down force, so pitch behavior depends on the design [[24:173|AFH 9-2]].

quiz.q: Your learner flies a long wing-low (sideslip) final. Which crosswind error does the AFH tie to the sideslip itself?
options: Floating long, because the lowered wing makes extra lift close to the runway
Excessive sink rate or too low an airspeed from the added drag and lost vertical lift
Overspeeding the flaps, because the sideslip adds airspeed as the bank increases
A tail stall, because the sideslip blanks the elevator whenever the flaps are down
quiz.why: The AFH crosswind error list includes excessive sink rate or too low an airspeed from increased drag and reduced vertical lift during sideslip [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].

quiz.q: Most reported midair collisions happen during which part of the pattern?
options: On the crosswind leg during the climb
On the 45-degree entry to downwind
On the upwind leg after a go-around
On final or short final
quiz.why: Most reported midair collisions occur on the final or short-final approach leg [[24:171|AFH 8-7]].

quiz.q: How does a slip feel to the pilot, according to the PHAK figure on sensations?
options: Like a level skid or an uncoordinated turn: pushed sideways in the seat
Like a coordinated turn: pressed straight down into the seat
Like a pull out: heavier, but with no sideways force at all
Like a gentle climb: pressed back into the seat without any sideways push
quiz.why: Skid, slip and uncoordinated turns feel similar; pilots feel forced sideways in the seat [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

quiz.q: What does the AIH say about learners who feel unfamiliar sensations in flight?
options: Push on, since repeated exposure in the same lesson is the quickest way through it
Don't ignore or ridicule it; understanding the cause usually overcomes it
Avoid the maneuver until the learner has 50 hours, and then try it again
Hand the learner to another instructor, since the reaction is a personality conflict
quiz.why: Instructors cannot ignore these sensations nor ridicule learners; they are usually overcome by understanding their causes [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

final_quiz.q: Runway 36, wind 040 at 12. Your learner is high on final and starts a forward slip. Which setup does the AFH call for?
options: Right wing down with left rudder, nose yawed off to the left of the runway
Left wing down with right rudder, nose yawed off to the right of the runway
Wings level, full left rudder only, so the nose points left of the runway
Right wing down with right rudder, a coordinated descending turn toward the wind
final_quiz.why: Wind from 040 is a right crosswind. Lower the upwind (right) wing so the airplane is banked into the wind, with opposite (left) rudder [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: Same approach, path now correct at 150 feet. What should the learner do with the controls to meet S7?
options: Level the wings and hold the forward slip's rudder until the nose swings back
Keep the forward slip until the mains touch, then straighten with nosewheel steering
Switch to a crab to the right and take it out with left rudder just above the runway
Set a sideslip: rudder lines the nose up, right wing stays low to stop drift
final_quiz.why: Transition to a sideslip: rudder aligns the nose with the runway, bank into the wind cancels drift [[24:187|AFH 9-16]]. Late transition to a sideslip is a listed error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

final_quiz.q: In the slip, the airspeed suddenly reads 70 knots against a target of 65, but the attitude and sound are the same as always. Your learner starts to raise the nose. Best coaching?
options: 'Good, raise the nose until the indicator reads 65, then hold that pitch'
'Add a little power so the speed stays steady while you slow down'
'Hold the attitude; in a slip the needle may be wrong, so use sound and feel'
'Take the slip out at once, because airspeed error means the pitot tube is blocked'
final_quiz.why: Some airspeed indicators have considerable error in a slip; recognize the slip by attitude, sound and feel [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Reacting to erroneous indications is a listed error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].

final_quiz.q: Your trainer's POH says to avoid slips with flaps more than 20 degrees. The learner is high with full flaps out on short final. Best choice?
options: Slip anyway; the POH note is a comfort item that the AFH tells pilots to ignore
Raise all the flaps at once, then slip, so the POH limit is no longer an issue
Lower the nose to the aiming point and dive at it, accepting 1,200 fpm to get down
Go around, or slip only within what the POH allows for that flap setting
final_quiz.why: The AFH says there may be limitations on slips with flaps and to consult the POH [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Diving builds excessive sink, and a go-around is the answer if the sink becomes excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: A real engine failure at 2,500 feet; you will overshoot the only field. The POH limits slips to 30 seconds. What does the AFH say?
options: Obey the 30-second limit no matter what, then fly straight and land long
The limit is irrelevant unless a prolonged slip caused the engine failure
Use flaps only, since a slip at idle is prohibited after an engine has failed
Restart attempts take priority, so slipping must wait until the restart has failed
final_quiz.why: In an actual engine-out emergency the time or fuel limit is irrelevant unless a prolonged slip caused the engine issue [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

final_quiz.q: At a field where the density altitude is 4,000 feet, with no wind, how does the landing compare with a sea-level field at the same weight and indicated speed?
options: Same indicated speed, higher true airspeed, roughly 14 percent more landing distance
Same true airspeed, lower indicated speed, and about the same landing distance
Higher indicated speed, same true airspeed, and about 4 percent more distance
Same indicated speed and same distance, because the braking force is unchanged
final_quiz.why: The airplane lands at the same IAS but a greater TAS; distance rises about 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet, so about 14 percent at 4,000 feet [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]].

final_quiz.q: Over a 50-foot tree line into a 2,200-foot strip, your learner plans a long forward slip to the threshold. What concern do you raise first?
options: None, since slips always shorten the landing roll on a short runway
The slip's drag will stop the airplane before it reaches the threshold
Removing the slip late leaves the airplane fast and floating with little runway
Slips are not allowed below 500 feet AGL at nontowered fields under the AIM traffic rules
final_quiz.why: Abrupt or late removal swings the nose and adds speed [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]; if the airplane will not touch down in the first third, go around [[24:203|AFH 9-32]].

final_quiz.q: A business jet has just made a low approach over your runway. Light quartering tailwind. You are on base and high. What does the AIM recommend?
options: Wait at least 2 minutes before landing behind its low approach
Slip steeply to get below the jet's path and land as early as possible
Land beyond the jet's rotation point and expect no wake at all
Land on the numbers because vortices always move upwind
final_quiz.why: After a larger aircraft's low approach, missed approach or touch-and-go, wait at least 2 minutes [[34:152|AIM 7-4-6]]; a light quartering tailwind can move vortices into the touchdown zone [[34:150|AIM 7-4-4]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner overshoots final in the base-to-final turn and pushes the inside rudder to 'slip it around.' What is really happening?
options: A sideslip, safe because a slip shows little yaw at the stall
A forward slip, which is the correct fix for an overshoot
A skidding cross-control setup; the AFH fix is a go-around
A coordinated turn, because the ball stays centered with inside rudder
final_quiz.why: Inside rudder with bank and back pressure is the skidding cross-control stall setup; the safest action for an overshoot is a go-around [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: During a slip demo, your learner asks why the slip stall is 'safer' if the AFH also warns about slipping turns. What is the accurate answer?
options: A slip cannot stall at all because the lowered wing is at a lower angle of attack
Little yaw at the stall, but in a slipping turn the outer wing may stall and drop
A stalled slip always rolls toward the lowered wing and then enters a spin
A stalled slip is only safe with flaps extended, which is why the POH requires them
final_quiz.why: A slip that stalls shows very little of the yawing tendency of a skid [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], yet in a slipping turn stall the outer wing may stall first and move down abruptly [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: At 250 feet AGL your learner is still in a full slip, sinking 1,200 fpm, and the aiming point keeps moving. What is the call?
options: Continue; the slip will be removed in the round out as the AFH describes
Add flaps now to reduce the sink rate before you reach 100 feet
Lower the nose to stop the aiming point from moving and keep slipping
Go around; the approach is unstabilized below 300 feet and the sink is excessive
final_quiz.why: Unstabilized below 300 feet AGL is an immediate go-around in a typical piston pattern [[24:177|AFH 9-6]]; 800 to 1,000 fpm or more is excessive [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

final_quiz.q: Winter morning, light rime ice on the leading edges after the climb. You planned slip demos with flaps. What does the icing guidance point to?
options: Fine to proceed; tail stalls only affect large transport jets in cruise
Be alert to tail stall after flaps go down; consider a no-flap landing per the AFM
Add full flaps early so the tail's angle of attack moves away from a stall
Slip harder with flaps extended to blow the ice off the horizontal tail before landing
final_quiz.why: Pilots should be alert to tailplane stall particularly after full flap deflection and consider a no-flap landing consistent with AFM procedures [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]]; with ice on the tail, flaps can raise the tail's negative AOA enough to stall it [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].

final_quiz.q: Tower offers 'cleared to land runway 27, hold short of runway 33' while you are teaching slips. Your learner has floated long on two of three tries. What do you do?
options: Decline promptly; only accept LAHSO when sure of stopping within the ALD
Accept; LAHSO removes the option to go around, which forces a good landing
Accept, and let the learner keep the slip in to the touchdown to stop quicker
Accept, then plan to cross runway 33 quickly if the airplane floats long
final_quiz.why: Accept LAHSO only if sure the airplane can land and stop within the Available Landing Distance [[33:253|AIM 4-3-11]] [[33:254|AIM 4-3-11]]; decline promptly if not [[33:255|AIM 4-3-11]].

takeaways: Forward slip loses height without adding speed; sideslip holds the centerline in a crosswind. Same inputs, different amount of rudder [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].
Your standard here is 400 feet beyond the point, no drift, axis aligned, the same window as the private Task (ACS AI.VII.M.S8).
In a crosswind, slip with the upwind wing low, then ease rudder into a sideslip before the round out [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Power idle, pitch for speed, and don't trust the airspeed needle in a slip: attitude, sound and feel [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Read the POH: slip time, fuel quantity and flap limits come first [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
Release the rudder smoothly and be out of the slip before the round out, or expect a fast float [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] [[24:186|AFH 9-15]].
A slip is a correction, not a rescue: excessive sink or an unstable approach below 300 feet is a go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]].
cfi_notes: The CFI Task is 'Slip to a Landing' with forward or side slip (ACS AI.VII.M.K1), while the private Task is 'Forward Slip to a Landing' (ACS PA.IV.M). Be ready to explain and fly both; examiners often ask the difference first.
This CFI landing Task keeps the 400-foot touchdown window (ACS AI.VII.M.S8), unlike the 200 feet of the CFI normal landing (ACS AI.VII.B.S10). Don't brief your own standard wrong.

Sources differ on slip stalls: AFH 9-13 says a stalled slip may do little more than roll toward wings level [[24:184|AFH 9-13]], but AFH 5-18 says in a slipping turn stall the outer wing may stall first and drop abruptly [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Teach both; the second is the honest caveat.

The 30-second slip limit and the note that it also applies to the wing-low crosswind method appear in the AFH's multiengine chapter, which says some single-engine airplanes have such limits too [[24:271|AFH 13-22]]. The single-engine slip section gives no number [[24:184|AFH 9-13]]. Brief the POH value, never 30 seconds as a rule.

R7 'tail stalls with flaps': for a clean airplane the sources only say there may be flap limits on slips 'for aerodynamic reasons' [[24:184|AFH 9-13]] and that flaps change the downwash and tail-down force [[24:173|AFH 9-2]]. Tailplane stall symptoms and recovery appear only in icing material [[23:93|IFH 4-16]] [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]]. Tell the examiner that honestly and teach the POH limit; don't present icing guidance as clean-wing slip guidance.
The AFH says flaps 'usually remain retracted' for the forward slip to a landing demonstration [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]. Many trainers allow some flaps; follow the POH and say which you are doing.
The AFH lists only forward slip errors [[24:186|AFH 9-15]]; for sideslip-to-landing errors use the crosswind error list in the same chapter [[24:191|AFH 9-20]].
The AFH uses 'student,' the AIH uses 'learner.' Same person.
gaps: Slip time limits, fuel quantity limits, flap limits for slips and approach speeds are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
No source gives the size or direction of the airspeed error in a slip for any airplane; it depends on pitot and static port placement [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].
No source explains how a slip itself changes the airflow over the tail, or gives a clean-airplane tail stall case; the mechanism is described only for ice-contaminated tails.
No source describes where a pilot should look during a forward slip when the nose is yawed away from the runway, or how the right-seat view differs. Build it in practice.
No source gives a crosswind limit specific to slips; the demonstrated crosswind and personal minimums apply [[24:190|AFH 9-19]] [[30:16|RMH 2-4]].

activities.title: Which slip is it?
activities.intro: Tap each statement, then tap the slip it describes.

items.t: The longitudinal axis stays parallel to the original flightpath
The nose points away from the direction of motion
Its main job is losing height without gaining speed
The airplane moves sideways toward the low wing to beat drift
Power is normally reduced to idle
Held through the touchdown and rollout in a crosswind
Removed when the round out begins
Just enough opposite rudder to prevent a turn

activities.title: Slip approach numbers
activities.intro: Work each one from the lesson's sources, then type your answer.

items.q: The examiner's point is 600 feet past the threshold. How far past the threshold is the far edge of your touchdown window?
items.why: Within 400 feet beyond or on the point (ACS AI.VII.M.S8): 600 + 400 = 1,000 feet.

items.q: Your learner exits the slip with the speed 10 percent above target and floats. POH landing distance is 1,250 feet. Using the PHAK's 20 percent figure for a 10 percent faster landing, about how much distance now?
items.why: An increase of landing speed by 10 percent increases landing distance by 20 percent [[1:273|PHAK 11-17]]: 1,250 x 1.2 = 1,500 feet.

items.q: Sea-level landing distance 1,300 feet. Using the PHAK's roughly 3.5 percent per 1,000 feet, about what distance at a 3,000-foot field?
Suppose your POH limits slips to 30 seconds. Slipping at 1,100 fpm, how much height can you lose within that limit?
items.why: 30 s is 0.5 min: 1,100 x 30 / 60 = 550 feet. Use your own POH number; 30 seconds is only the AFH's example [[24:271|AFH 13-22]].

activities.title: The AFH slip-to-landing pattern
activities.intro: Put the demonstration in order, then tap Check.
steps: Downwind, flaps usually retracted, before-landing checks done
Abeam the landing point: power to idle
If the descent on downwind is not enough, forward slip
Coordinated turn to base; if still high, keep slipping
Coordinated turn to line up with final
Forward slip to set the path to the aiming point
At the round out, remove the slip and make a normal landing

activities.title: Read the sideslip
activities.intro: Drag each name to its pin on the sideslip approach.

pins.label: Centerline the nose is aligned with

activities.title: True or false: slip limits and indications
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Some airplanes limit slips because fuel can flow away from the tank pickup in uncoordinated flight.
cards.why: True. The limits are meant to preclude fuel starvation [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

cards.s: The AFH says a slip with flaps extended is always approved if the airspeed is below the flap limit speed.
cards.why: False. There may be recommendations or limitations on slips with flaps; consult the POH [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

cards.s: With ice on the tail, a tailplane stall gives a sudden nose-down pitch, and the IFH recovery starts with retracting the flaps to the previous setting.
cards.why: True. The IFH lists sudden uncommanded nose-down pitch as a tailplane icing symptom; retract the flaps to the previous setting with nose-up elevator [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]. This is icing guidance, not a clean-airplane rule.

cards.s: In a slip, the airspeed indicator is always the best cue for holding approach speed.
cards.why: False. Some indicators have considerable error in a slip; use attitude, sound and feel [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

cards.s: Installation and instrument errors in the airspeed indicator are generally greatest at low airspeeds.
cards.why: True. They may total several knots and are generally greatest at low airspeeds [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

cards.s: When the nose is raised in a slip, rudder effectiveness increases, so the bank can be steepened.
cards.why: False. Raising the nose reduces rudder effectiveness, so reduce the bank [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

activities.title: Slip lesson on a gusty afternoon
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner is practicing slips to a landing on runway 18 with the wind from 220 at 12. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: Before turning final the learner is clearly high. Which wing do you expect them to lower?
options: Left wing, with right rudder
Right wing, with left rudder
Neither; crab first and slip later
Whichever feels more comfortable
steps.why: Wind from 220 on runway 18 is from the right; lower the upwind wing [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

steps.s: In the slip the learner adds a little power 'to stay smooth.' What do you say?
options: 'Good, keep it there'
'Power to idle; let the slip take off the height'
'Add more power and steepen the slip'
'Use the power to hold the airspeed needle'
steps.why: Using excess power while trying to lose altitude is a listed error; power is normally idle [[24:186|AFH 9-15]] [[24:184|AFH 9-13]].

steps.s: At 200 feet the airspeed indication drops 10 knots in a gust and the learner pushes forward hard. The sink rate jumps past 1,000 fpm. Your call?
options: 'Pull up to correct it'
'Steepen the slip'
'Go around'
'Lower some flaps'
steps.why: Unstable below 300 feet AGL and an excessive sink rate call for a go-around [[24:177|AFH 9-6]] [[24:201|AFH 9-30]].

steps.s: Next approach is good. At 50 feet the nose is still yawed well left of the runway. What do you prompt?
options: 'Nose to the runway, keep the right wing down'
'Hold it, we'll straighten on the ground'
'Level the wings now'
'More left rudder'
steps.why: Transition to a sideslip before touchdown; landing with the axis not parallel is an error [[24:186|AFH 9-15]] [[24:187|AFH 9-16]].

steps.s: Your learner is tense and talking fast on final. How much do you say?
options: Full explanations to calm them
Nothing until the debrief
Short, concise prompts only
A quiz on the POH limits
steps.why: Excessive coaching on final can cause missed calls and less traffic awareness; use only concise prompting [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
